title: Saussure and Structuralism
description: Sign, langue and parole, Lévi-Strauss and the structural method

concepts.title: Saussure's Sign
concepts.contentHtml:
Ferdinand de Saussure's Course in General Linguistics (compiled posthumously in 1916 from student notes) supplied the basic vocabulary of twentieth-century structural thought.

A linguistic sign unites a signifier (a sound-image, e.g. the spoken or written 'tree') with a signified (the concept, the idea of tree). The relation is arbitrary: there is no natural reason that this sound goes with this concept — different languages pair them differently.

What gives a sign its identity is therefore not its bond to a thing in the world but its differences from other signs. 'Tree' is what it is by not being 'shrub', 'plant', 'forest'. Meaning emerges from a system of differences, not from a stock of positive contents.

concepts.title: Langue and Parole
concepts.contentHtml:
Saussure distinguishes langue — the abstract system of language as a structure of relations — from parole, individual concrete speech acts. Linguistics, he proposes, should take langue as its object: the system that any speech act presupposes.

This shifts the focus from historical (diachronic) study of how words evolved to the synchronic analysis of how the system functions at a moment. A chess analogy: the meaning of a piece is given by its place in the rules, not by its history of being carved.

The langue/parole distinction becomes a template for structuralism across many fields: study the system of relations rather than the individual instance; the structure rather than the event.

concepts.title: Lévi-Strauss and the Structural Method
concepts.contentHtml:
Claude Lévi-Strauss (1908–2009) imported Saussure into anthropology. Myths, kinship systems, food taboos — apparently bewildering surface diversity — could be analysed as combinations of underlying structural oppositions: raw/cooked, nature/culture, life/death.

In The Elementary Structures of Kinship (1949) he treated marriage rules as exchange systems whose deep grammar resembles the phonological structure of language. In the four-volume Mythologiques, myths from across the Americas are decoded as transformations of one another, working out logical contradictions through narrative.

Structuralism's appeal was its rigour: human cultures were not chaotic surfaces but generated by underlying systems of relations that the analyst could uncover. By the 1960s the method had spread to Roland Barthes (literature, fashion, mythology), Lacan (psychoanalysis), Althusser (Marxism), and Foucault (early works).

title: Derrida and Deconstruction
description: Différance, the metaphysics of presence, and reading against the grain

concepts.title: From Structure to Différance
concepts.contentHtml:
Jacques Derrida (1930–2004) launched what came to be called poststructuralism with three books in 1967, including Of Grammatology. His starting point is a sympathetic but radical critique of Saussure.

Saussure rightly saw that meaning is differential. But he then privileged the spoken sign over writing, treating speech as the natural and immediate form of language and writing as a derivative copy. Derrida argues this betrays the differential principle: speech, no less than writing, depends on differences, traces, and the play of signifiers.

His coined term différance (with an 'a') gathers two senses: to differ (signs are what they are by differing from others) and to defer (meaning is never fully present in any moment but always referred to other signs). There is no point at which the chain of signification halts in pure presence.

concepts.title: The Metaphysics of Presence
concepts.contentHtml:
Derrida diagnoses Western philosophy from Plato onward as a metaphysics of presence: the persistent assumption that meaning, being, or truth must somewhere be fully present to itself.

Examples: Plato's Forms (the eidos as full being), Descartes' cogito (the self-presence of consciousness), Husserl's living present (the now of intentional consciousness). Each posits a privileged moment of immediacy that grounds all derivative phenomena.

Derrida argues this hierarchy cannot hold up to its own criteria. The privileged term — speech over writing, presence over absence, originality over repetition — turns out to depend on what it claimed to exclude. This is the core deconstructive insight: the supposedly fundamental term is constituted by its supposedly derivative other.

concepts.title: Reading and Iteration
concepts.contentHtml:
Deconstruction is not a method one applies but a way of reading texts that exposes the way they undo themselves. A close reading reveals that the author's official thesis depends on assumptions and metaphors that contradict it; the text is divided against itself.

Derrida emphasises iterability: any sign must be repeatable in new contexts, including ones the original speaker did not foresee. Every utterance is haunted by its possible repetition; meaning depends on this repeatability and so cannot be controlled by any single intention.

The political and ethical resonances are wide. Hierarchies — speech/writing, reason/emotion, masculine/feminine, West/non-West — operate by similar exclusions, and exposing their internal instability is part of what deconstruction does. But Derrida insists deconstruction is not destruction or relativism: it is a vigilance about how texts and institutions secretly depend on what they exclude.

title: Foucault: Discourse, Power, Biopolitics
description: Archaeology, genealogy, the panopticon, and the deployment of sexuality

concepts.title: Archaeology of Knowledge
concepts.contentHtml:
Michel Foucault (1926–1984) began his work as historical investigations of strange archives: psychiatric records, medical institutions, scientific classifications. The Order of Things (1966) introduces the term episteme — the historical a priori that defines, for a given period, what counts as knowledge.

Different epochs do not merely have different theories within a stable framework; they have different orders of intelligibility. The Renaissance worked by resemblance and signatures; the Classical age (17th–18th c.) by representation and table; the modern by depth, history, and life.

The 'archaeology' digs beneath stated theories to the rules of formation governing what statements can be made, what counts as evidence, what objects of knowledge can exist. The history of ideas becomes a history of the discursive conditions of knowing itself.

concepts.title: Power-Knowledge and Discipline
concepts.contentHtml:
From the 1970s Foucault turned to genealogy: a Nietzschean history of the present that traces how present categories were forged in struggles for power.

Discipline and Punish (1975) reads the modern prison as part of a wider 'disciplinary' apparatus emerging in the 18th–19th centuries. Schools, factories, barracks, hospitals — all use timetables, examinations, surveillance, normalising judgement. Bentham's panopticon (an architectural design for total visibility of inmates) becomes the emblem of a power that operates through visibility and self-monitoring.

The slogan power-knowledge captures the thesis: knowledge is not neutral discovery but is bound up with power that produces objects of knowledge (the criminal, the patient, the pupil) and subjects who internalise the gaze. Power, for Foucault, is not only repressive — it is productive: it makes selves of certain kinds.

concepts.title: Biopolitics and the Care of the Self
concepts.contentHtml:
The first volume of The History of Sexuality (1976) opens with a famous critique of the 'repressive hypothesis': the idea that the Victorians silenced sex which the moderns now liberate. Foucault inverts this. The 19th century did not silence sex but generated an explosion of discourse on it — confessional, medical, psychiatric, juridical — producing sexuality as a domain of knowledge and a category of identity.

From there Foucault develops the concept of biopower: a modern form of power directed at populations and life itself, optimising birth rates, health, longevity, productivity. Where sovereign power had taken life or let live, biopower 'makes live and lets die'.

His final lectures and the second and third volumes of The History of Sexuality turned to the care of the self in Greek and Roman antiquity — practices by which subjects work on themselves to become certain kinds of self. The genealogy of subjectivity completes his programme: showing how selves are not given but historically produced.

title: Deleuze and Guattari
description: Rhizome, desiring-machines, body without organs, assemblage

concepts.title: Difference and Repetition
concepts.contentHtml:
Gilles Deleuze (1925–1995) wrote Difference and Repetition (1968), a philosophical attack on what he called the dogmatic image of thought. Western philosophy, he argues, has subordinated difference to identity: difference is treated as the gap between things that are presupposed as already self-identical.

Deleuze proposes the reverse: difference is primary, identity is a special, derived case. Beneath the world of distinct objects lies a continuum of intensive differences — gradients, thresholds, becomings. Repetition is not the return of the same but the variation in which difference works itself out.

This metaphysics draws on Spinoza, Nietzsche, Bergson, and Hume rather than the Hegelian tradition. It refuses dialectic, with its negation and resolution, in favour of affirmation and creation.

concepts.title: Anti-Oedipus and Desiring-Machines
concepts.contentHtml:
With the radical psychoanalyst Félix Guattari (1930–1992), Deleuze wrote Anti-Oedipus (1972), a polemical fusion of philosophy, psychoanalysis, and political economy.

Their target is the Oedipal triangle — daddy-mommy-me — which they accuse Freud and Lacan of treating as the universal grammar of desire. Desire, Deleuze and Guattari argue, is not a private drama of lack but a productive social force, a network of desiring-machines that connect, cut, and flow across bodies and institutions.

Capitalism is ambivalent. It deterritorialises every code, freeing flows of desire from traditional containers; but it reterritorialises them onto private property, the family, the nation-state. Schizoanalysis, their proposed alternative to psychoanalysis, asks how desire can flow without being recaptured.

concepts.title: A Thousand Plateaus and the Rhizome
concepts.contentHtml:
The companion volume A Thousand Plateaus (1980) develops a vocabulary that has become widely influential.

The rhizome is opposed to the tree. A tree has a single root, a hierarchy of branches; a rhizome (like couch grass or ginger) sends out shoots that connect anywhere and re-emerge anywhere. Knowledge, history, even subjectivity should be analysed as rhizomatic networks rather than tree-like structures.

An assemblage (agencement) is a heterogeneous collection — bodies, words, institutions, machines — that holds together through what it does. A courtroom, a beehive, a city block: each is an assemblage. Deterritorialisation names the breaking-loose of components from a coding; reterritorialisation, their reconnection on new terms.

The body without organs is not a body lacking organs but a body that has reached a state of pure intensity, freed from the rigid organisation imposed by 'organism'. The vocabulary aims at thinking processes of becoming rather than fixed substances.

title: Lyotard, Baudrillard, Lacan
description: Postmodern condition, simulacra, and the symbolic order

concepts.title: Lyotard and the Postmodern Condition
concepts.contentHtml:
Jean-François Lyotard (1924–1998) wrote The Postmodern Condition (1979) for the Council of Universities of Quebec — a short report that became a defining statement of postmodernism.

The thesis: the modern era was sustained by metanarratives (grands récits) — overarching stories that legitimated knowledge and politics. Examples: the Enlightenment story of progressive emancipation through reason; the Hegelian-Marxist story of dialectical history; the speculative narrative that all knowledge will be unified.

The postmodern condition is defined by 'incredulity toward metanarratives'. Knowledge, art, and politics fragment into local language games. Lyotard does not lament this: he sees it as opening room for plurality, dissent, and the differend — disputes that cannot be settled by appeal to a shared rule because the rule itself is contested.

concepts.title: Baudrillard and the Hyperreal
concepts.contentHtml:
Jean Baudrillard (1929–2007) pushed the analysis of signs into a theory of media-saturated society. In Simulacra and Simulation (1981) he distinguishes four orders of the image:

1. The image reflects a reality. 2. It masks and distorts a reality. 3. It masks the absence of a reality. 4. It bears no relation to any reality whatever — it is its own pure simulacrum.

In late capitalist media, signs no longer represent things; they refer only to other signs. The result is hyperreality — a world in which the model precedes and replaces the real. Disneyland, opinion polls, theme-park history: each circulates without an original it could be checked against.

Baudrillard's claim that 'the Gulf War did not take place' (1991) was a provocative application: the war existed, but for Western audiences it appeared as a media simulation, an extension of the screen rather than an encounter with the real.

concepts.title: Lacan: The Mirror, the Symbolic, the Real
concepts.contentHtml:
Jacques Lacan (1901–1981) reread Freud through Saussure and Hegel. His three orders structure psychic life:

The Imaginary: the realm of images, identifications, and the ego. The famous mirror stage describes how the infant, around 6–18 months, identifies with its mirror image — a unified picture that masks its actual fragmented bodily experience. The ego is born in this misrecognition.

The Symbolic: the order of language, law, and social roles, structured by signifiers. The unconscious is 'structured like a language'; we become subjects by entering this order, whose central operator Lacan calls the Name-of-the-Father.

The Real: not external reality but what resists symbolisation — the trauma, the impasse, the gap in the symbolic. Lacanian psychoanalysis works at the points where the symbolic fails to capture the subject's desire, and where the ineradicable Real returns.
